vignette:
He is 54, a European man who has spent most of his adult life working as a civil servant, the kind of person colleagues describe as steady, polite, and unflappable. He takes pride in order: files where they belong, meetings prepared for, forms completed correctly the first time. For years, that carefulness also shapes his private life. He is in a long-term relationship, and at first he understands his partner's volatility as stress, then as sensitivity, then as something he can manage if he is patient enough and calm enough. He becomes skilled at reading the atmosphere in the flat the moment he opens the door.

The first time she hits him, they are arguing about something small and forgettable, a bill left unpaid, a comment he made that she hears as criticism. He remembers mostly the shock of it, not the pain. A slap, then a second blow with the heel of her hand when he turns away. He stands still, stunned, feeling less injured than disoriented. She cries soon afterward and tells him she has never done that before, that she is under pressure, that he knows how to push her buttons. He accepts the apology quickly. He does not tell anyone. It seems impossible, even absurd, to imagine saying out loud that his partner has hit him.

After that, the violence arrives unpredictably. Sometimes it is shoving him into a doorway, sometimes fists against his upper arm or chest, once a heavy mug thrown past his head that shatters against the wall behind him. The worst episodes seem to come out of nowhere, though later he can always identify the signs he missed: the clipped answers, the pacing, the accusation already forming. He learns to keep his voice even and his body still. He monitors her face while speaking, edits himself mid-sentence, avoids topics that might ignite her. When arguments begin, he feels his thoughts narrow. His heart races, his skin prickles, and a familiar conviction takes hold that he must get through the next few minutes without making anything worse.

He still goes to work each day, ironed shirt, tidy desk, measured tone. In the office he can lose himself for stretches of time in policy documents and procedural notes, and there is relief in the predictability of institutional language. But the strain shows at the edges. If someone raises a voice in a meeting, his shoulders tense before he can stop them. When a door slams along the corridor, he jolts upright, pulse suddenly pounding. He begins checking his phone repeatedly during the day, worried about what messages might be waiting: accusations, demands, threats to leave, threats to hurt herself, threats about what will happen when he gets home. He struggles to concentrate and finds himself rereading the same paragraph several times without taking it in.

At night he sleeps lightly. The smallest sound in the flat can pull him awake into instant alertness, his body braced before his mind catches up. Sometimes he lies there listening for her footsteps, trying to judge from the rhythm whether she is angry. Sometimes he dreams of being trapped in the hallway outside their bedroom, unable to move while she comes toward him. He wakes sweating, ashamed of his fear and angry at himself for staying. In the mornings he studies his reflection for marks he can explain. Long sleeves become habitual. He tells himself he is tired because of work.

What unsettles him most is how much his world shrinks. He stops seeing friends as often because he does not want to answer questions, and because leaving the house can trigger suspicion and another confrontation. His partner alternates between remorse and contempt. In gentler moments she is affectionate, almost unbearably so, and he feels guilty for thinking of leaving. In violent moments she calls him weak, pathetic, less of a man for being afraid of her. Those words lodge in him. He starts to believe that being injured by a partner is somehow humiliating in a way he should have been able to prevent.

Now, even when there is no argument underway, he lives as if one might begin at any second. He notices where the exits are in every room. He keeps his tone neutral, his movements deliberate. Loud voices in public make his stomach tighten. When his current partner reaches for him unexpectedly, even kindly, his body can flinch before he recognizes the touch. He is embarrassed by this and tries to hide it, laughing it off, but afterward he feels shaken and distant. There are times during the day when an image flashes into his mind-the mug hitting the wall, her face changing, the instant before a blow-and for a moment he is back there completely, body rigid, breath held.

He speaks about the abuse quietly, as if testing whether the words can exist outside him without causing damage. What comes through most strongly is not only fear, but the exhaustion of having organized his whole life around avoiding another assault. He says he used to think of home as the place where he put himself back together after work. Now he sits in his car for several minutes before going inside, hands on the steering wheel, trying to steady himself for whatever version of the evening is waiting beyond the front door.
